from the management, Mr. Sharad Mahendra, Joint MD and CEO; Mr. Chandrasekaran

Sharad Mahendra: 
Thank you, Ishan. Good evening, everyone, and thank you for joining us for JSW Energy's Q2 
FY27 earnings call. I hope you and your families are keeping well.  
                                                At the outset, let me start with the fact, that the fundamentals of our sector have never looked 
this stronger. If I were to sum up this quarter in one line, it would be this: the market is moving 
towards exactly what we have been building. Three themes defined the sector over the last three 
months. Demand kept beating expectations on the back of a strong economy, energy security 
moved to the centre of the national agenda, and procurement shifted decisively towards firm, 
reliable power. Let me take each of these in turn, and then show you how JSW Energy is 
positioned on each. 
                                                The first is demand, and it rests on a resilient economy. India continues to be among the fastest-
growing major economies in the world. Real GDP grew 7.8% year-on-year in Q1 FY27, and the 
RBI expects growth to remain robust at about 7.1% for FY27. High-frequency indicators point 
to sustained momentum: the Index of Industrial Production grew 8% year-on-year in August, 
PMIs rebounded in September to 55.1 for manufacturing and 55.2 for services, well within 
expansion territory, and GST collections rose about 7.7% year-on-year to ₹6.15 trillion in Q2 
FY27. 
                                                This economic momentum is translating directly into electricity consumption. Power demand in 
Q2 FY27 grew about 11.1% year-on-year, building on 8.3% growth in Q1. September alone 
grew about 11.3%, with peak demand touching 270 GW in Q2FY27. The momentum 
strengthened further into October, with month-to-date demand growth of 21.2%. 
                                                Part of this is weather, as monsoon was about 13% below normal in Q2FY27 and cooling 
demand stayed high well into the evening. But the larger drivers are structural and, in our view, 
durable: industrialisation, urbanisation, rising per capita consumption, and new sources of load 
such as data centres and electric mobility. These support our view of a 5–6% long-term CAGR 
in power demand, and the last two quarters suggest that view may prove conservative.

                                               The second theme is energy security. The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has disrupted LNG 
and crude flows through the Strait of Hormuz, tightened global energy markets and pushed 
utilities across Asia back towards coal. For India, the priority is clear: secure, domestically 
sourced, dispatchable power, backed by a domestic manufacturing base, is no longer optional. 
It is a strategic necessity. 
                                                The sharp rise in imported coal prices has significantly impacted fuel costs across the sector. 
API4 benchmark coal prices averaged close to US$115 per tonne in Q2 FY27, up around 28% 
year-on-year from US$90 per tonne. Despite this increase, our transition to domestic coal and 
the implementation of job-work arrangements at imported-coal plants, which shield us from 
fuel-price volatility, have enabled us to effectively mitigate the impact and maintain cost 
competitiveness. 
                                                Domestic supply has also tightened. Coal stocks at power plants fell to multi-year lows, and in 
October around 96 plants were classified as critical, holding an average of 6–7 days of stock 
against the normative 19–20 days.  
                                                Tight fuel supply, coupled with robust demand, flowed directly through to the power exchanges. 
Day-Ahead Market prices averaged ₹5.7 per unit in Q2 FY27. Our merchant realisation, 
however, stood around ₹6.9 per unit which was around 20% higher than the DAM average, 
driven by the strategic bilateral contracts we have entered into. 
                                                The third theme is the shift towards firm power. On the supply side, capacity addition continues 
at a record pace. India added about 23.9 GW of renewables in the first half of FY27, including 
20.8 GW of solar, taking non-fossil capacity past 300 GW. On the thermal side, about 3.3 GW 
was net commissioned in H1, with about 39 GW under construction. 
                                                But the more telling signal is in the bidding. Renewables still dominate new capacity additions, 
yet procurement is shifting decisively towards firm and dispatchable capacity: FDRE, solar-
plus-storage, standalone batteries and, notably, long-term thermal. States awarded around 17 
GW of long-term thermal capacity at tariffs of about ₹5.4 to ₹6.3 per unit in FY26, and a further 
18 GW of thermal tenders are currently under bidding. To us, the conclusion is simple. 
Renewables and thermal are not competing; they are complementary. Renewables deliver the 
cheapest energy, while thermal and storage keep the lights on through the evening peak. 
                                                Let me now connect each of these three themes, demand, energy security and firm power, to 
what we executed this quarter.  
                                                Since April, we have commissioned 1.4 GW of organic renewable capacity as compared to last 
full year’s approximately 1.2 GW. This is also nearly half of our FY27 target of 3 GW. In Q2, 
we added 513 MW, comprising 301 MW of solar and 212 MW of hybrid capacity. Including the 
300 MW Maruti thermal acquisition, total capacity additions since April stand at 1.7 GW, taking 
our installed capacity above 15.1 GW, with renewables accounting for approximately 61% of 
the portfolio.

                                                On the remaining 1.6 GW, we are fully on track. Land and transmission connectivity are secured, 
equipment is either on site or in transit, and offtake is backed by long-term PPAs. The pipeline 
is substantially de-risked, and we are confident of achieving our 3 GW commissioning target for 
FY27, supported by planned capex of around ₹20,000 crore. Further, on our energy storage 
pursuits, we expect to commission about 1 GWh of projects in FY27. 
                                               We are also enthused by the sizeable C&I opportunity in the market, and particularly by the 
opportunity within our own Group as its companies pursue ambitious growth plans. Our installed 
C&I portfolio, including group captive, stands at 3.7 GW, about 25% of our total operating 
capacity. We expect it to grow to over 8.5 GW by 2030, with Group companies contributing a 
large share. 
                                                JSW Energy has long been the energy partner of choice for the JSW Group, meeting around 3 
GW of round-the-clock thermal and renewable power demand across Group companies. That 
partnership has the potential to have a significant step-up. With JSW Steel planning to expand 
capacity to up to 80 MTPA, and other Group businesses scaling rapidly, the Group’s RTC power 
requirement is expected to more than double to around 7 GW by 2032. A substantial share of 
this will be met through green energy, in line with the Group’s decarbonisation ambitions. 
                                                We have already laid the groundwork to capture this demand. Of the 6.2 GW of MoUs signed 
with Group companies in Q2FY24, 4.5 GW is yet to be tied up, and 2 GW of this is under 
advanced discussion. This represents a large, visible and high-quality growth pipeline. JSW 
Energy is well positioned to serve as an integrated energy partner to the Group and to the wider 
industrial market, delivering reliable, round-the-clock and increasingly green power at scale. 
This will add a strong layer of long-term, assured demand to our growth trajectory. 
                                                Looking further ahead, our locked-in pipeline gives us clear line of sight to our 30 GW target 
for 2030, and our growth runway extends well beyond it. Multiple drivers support our growth 
beyond 2030: the Salboni thermal project; the 920 MW Punatsangchhu-III hydro project, our 
first cross-border generation venture, being developed in partnership with Druk Green Power 
Corporation, Bhutan’s state-owned utility; and further thermal & C&I opportunities. Meanwhile, 
our sizeable pumped storage pipeline of about 26.4 GWh remains on track. 
                                                Moving ahead, As the market pays more for firm power, we have strengthened our thermal 
platform in two ways. 
                                                First, by buying value. We completed the acquisition of Maruti Clean Coal & Power in August 
at an enterprise value of ₹1,410 crore. It is EBITDA and PAT accretive from day one and lowers 
our net leverage. About 195 MW (net) is tied up under a long-term PPA with Rajasthan discoms 
with around 14 years of residual life, while about 64 MW gives us merchant exposure at a time 
of strong prices. In Q2, this plant generated about ₹45 crore of EBITDA in just 55 days, from 
our acquisition on August 6th to the end of the quarter. 
                                                Second, by building at low cost. At Salboni, Turbine Generator orders for all four 800 MW units, 
totalling 3,200 MW, are now in place, with the Phase II turbines ordered from Toshiba JSW in 
September. Site work on Phase I is progressing well, and the first unit is expected by 2030. At 
KSK, the 600 MW fourth unit remains on track for FY28, and the balance 1,200 MW by FY29.

                                                On fuel, our continued shift to domestic coal has insulated us from the rise in imported prices, 
as I said earlier. Recently acquired Maruti Thermal Plant is also fully domestically fuelled, 
through a long-term Fuel Supply Agreement with SECL and linkage under the SHAKTI scheme. 
                                                Coming on to our thermal growth ambition, as you know, we raised our stake in Toshiba JSW 
Power Systems to 10.7% in July. The scheme to acquire GE Power India's boiler business, 
including its Durgapur manufacturing facility, received NCLT sanction on October 1st, and the 
transaction should close soon. We have placed the boiler order for the entire Salboni project with 
the Durgapur facility, which sits in the same state as the project. With turbines from Toshiba 
JSW and boilers from our own facility, we now control the critical path of our thermal build-
out, at one of the lowest capital costs in the industry and on one of the shortest timelines. 
                                                The same logic applies to renewables. Our Halol wind blade facility has been producing blades 
for our wind projects since its commissioning in June, and the Chitradurga facility remains on 
track for completion in Q3 FY27. 
                                                Further, I am also pleased to share that ICRA and India Ratings have affirmed JSW Energy's 
long-term credit rating at AA with a Stable outlook. This recognises our larger and more 
diversified operating base, our high share of contracted capacity, and the deleveraging we 
delivered through the ₹10,150 crore capital unlocking in this calendar year. A stronger rating 
directly helps contain our cost of capital as we fund our ongoing leg of growth. 
                                                I’d also like to address curtailment, an issue the sector as a whole is grappling with. Curtailment 
across our portfolio stood at about 4.8% of total generation in H1, below the national level 
curtailment of about 5.4%. In Q2, our curtailed units stood at ~225 MUs with a Revenue impact 
of Rupees 59 Crores. Further, about 60% of our curtailed capacity currently on temporary GNA 
will move to permanent GNA by the end of Q3 FY27, which should reduce our exposure 
meaningfully. 
                                                Our growing renewable portfolio also helped us avoid about 13 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions 
in H1 FY27 and about 8.4 million tonnes in Q2 FY27, based on the prevailing Indian grid 
emission factor. 
                                                Coming to our Q2 operational performance.  
                                                Net generation for Q2 FY27 increased by 17% year-on-year to 17.5 billion units, driven by 
robust capacity addition and healthy plant performance. 
                                                On hydro, the monsoon was weaker this year, and All-India hydro generation declined about 
15% year-on-year in Q2. Our plants held up well against this backdrop, helped by their location 
in the Sutlej and Ravi basins, which outperformed the national trend. In the Sutlej basin, 
Karcham Wangtoo and Baspa did broadly comparable to the basin, operating at consolidated 
PLF of about 90%. In the Ravi basin, where generation rose about 14%, Kutehr more than 
doubled its generation to about 408 million units in its first full monsoon season, at a PLF of 
about 78%. Our Tidong plant, which was commissioned in Q1FY27 before the scheduled 
timeline of October 2026, gave us a healthy advantage of ongoing hydro season – the plant 
generated 199 MUs in Q2FY27 at a PLF of 61%. Overall, driven by incremental generation from 
Kutehr and Tidong, our hydro generation was 3,421 million units, up 13% year-on-year.

                                                On thermal, generation was 8.9 billion units, up 13% year-on-year, including 321 million units 
from the newly acquired Maruti plant. Our consolidated thermal PLF was 75% in Q2, against 
the All-India thermal PLF of 67.8%. Mahanadi operated at 90% PLF, and Utkal continued stable 
supply under its PPAs with Karnataka and Assam, at a PLF of 82%. Utkal had an exceptional

year to ₹368 crore in Q2 FY27, and grew over 60% YoY in H1 FY27. This was driven by 
significantly better plant performance and by PPA realisations well above the DAM prices at 
which the plant’s power was sold a year ago. 
                                                On renewables, All-India generation grew about 11% year-on-year for wind and about 39% for 
solar in Q2, driven largely by capacity additions, with All-India PLFs of about 37% for wind 
and 18% for solar. Our wind and solar portfolios operated at PLFs of 46% and 19% respectively, 
and generation was up 25% for wind and 36% for solar, supported by a year-on-year capacity 
increase of ~1.5 GW. 
                                                Turning to our financials, many of which you will already be familiar with from the pre-call 
materials. Backed by robust capacity addition and healthy plant performance, revenue for the 
quarter was ₹6,658 crore, up 24% year-on-year, and EBITDA was ₹3,907 crore, up 23% year-
on-year. 
                                                With year-on-year capacity addition of ~1.9 GW and new assets being capitalised, depreciation 
rose 17% to ₹943 crore, and finance costs rose 14% to ₹1,615 crore, in line with the pace of 
capacity we are adding. Further, I’m sure many of you have questions about the potential 
increase in interest rate due to the recent actions by RBI and the inflationary expectations, and 
what they could mean for our bottom line. Our debt book is well insulated. Close to a quarter of 
our term debt is at fixed rates, and nearly 90% of the floating portion is linked to lenders’ internal 
benchmarks like MCLR, rather than Repo or other market linked instruments like Treasury-bills 
etc. Historically, we have seen that MCLRs tend to lag and not increase in the same quantum as 
that of Repo. We also actively and progressively keep pursuing refinancing as our projects reach 
commissioning and build operating track records. With that lever of refinancing  still available 
and lag in MCLR reset, we do not see any immediate rise in debt cost, and may be only a modest 
impact, in the medium term, if the interest rates hikes continues.  
                                                Additionally, as you can see in our presentation, our Debt cost has come down significantly by 
about 51 bps to 8.28%, from about 8.79%, a year back.  
                                                Profit After Tax was ₹1,141 crore, up 38% year-on-year, and PAT attributable to shareholders 
was ₹1,056 crore, up 50% YoY. 
                                                Excluding debt tied to capital work-in-progress, our Net Debt to TTM EBITDA stands at about 
4.94 times, down from about 5.2 times in FY26. We hold cash and cash equivalents of about 
₹15,700 crore, and our cash return on net worth, adjusted for our JSW Steel shareholding, stands 
at about 15%.

                                                Let me return to where I started. The economy is growing strongly, and power demand is 
growing even faster. Energy security is now national policy, and the market is rewarding firm, 
reliable power. 
                                                JSW Energy is well positioned on each of these fronts. We have a portfolio diversified across 
modes such as Thermal, Hydro, Wind and Solar, backed by an increasingly integrated supply

                                                Overall, we enter the second half of the year with confidence and momentum.  
                                                As we approach Diwali, I would also like to extend warm wishes to all of you and your families 
for a joyous festive season and a prosperous year ahead. Thank you, and we look forward to
